Occurrence Remarks: This is Allocasuarina littoralis - from the genus Allocasuarina and from the family Casuarinaceae. The family Casuarinaceae has trees with slender, wire-like branchlets. The species in this family also produce cones as fruits. While no flowers are present at the time of observation, some of the plants’ inflorescences had developed into woody structures - cones. In this family, there are only two genus - Allocasuarina and Casuarina. This species does not belong in the genus Casuarina as it seems that its cones do not have a spherical/oval shape which species from the genus Casuarina have. Allocasuarina littoralis is a species with long branchlets. Its cones grow from a short stalk/peduncle. The cones are dark brown to black in colour, and its diameter is rarely longer than its length.
Trees 30 feet [9.1m]. Bark furrowed. These fruits typical of one tree only, others smaller.
Small tree, to c. 5 m high; branchlets thin, with 6-8 leaf teeth; fruit 15-20 mm diam, at abse of branchlets.

Occurrence Remarks: Using the description provided by PlantNET the plant would be: In the family Thymelaeaceae because they have a bisexual, actinomorphic and ovary superior flower that has 6 stamen and a three lobed style. In the genus Burchardia as they have elongated basal leaves that are folded lengthwise and have their inflorescence in an umbel. In the species Burchardia umbellata as they are the only species in the genus that is found in NSW. Additionally it’s location matched their general habitat as they were adjacent to a lagoon

(Monocot) The number of flower bases is 6, indicating that the plant is a monocot. The flowers are whorled and arranged regularly, strictly related to the number of flower bases. The flowers are in the same perianth, showing strong characteristics of Liliales. After several identifications with plant identification software, it is almost certain that it is Colchicumaceae, a family that has recently branched from Liliaceae. Since there are no leaves, it is impossible to search through the key table of Colchicumaceae in plantnet, and Robinson Book does not even record this family (or maybe I can't find it), so we used the results of plant identification software to further search and found that Genus Burchardia is characterized by perennial herbs, smooth and hairless, with bulbs with papery scales, and tuberous roots. The leaves are mostly basal, 1 to 5, and folded. The scape is simple or has 1 to 4 branches, 1 to 4 bracts, and the inflorescence is umbrella-shaped, with up to 20 flowers or single flowers. The flowers are bisexual, with 6 tepals arranged in a whorl, similar and independent. There are 6 stamens, with anthers dorsifixed and split longitudinally, spreading outward. The ovary is superior, 3-chambered, with multiple ovules in each chamber, and the style is short and 3-lobed. The fruit is a capsule, with angular, brown seeds. In addition to these descriptions, the illustrations and pictures provided by plantnet also provide some hints. This information is almost completely consistent with our plant, with no discrepancies. So we think it belongs to the genus burchardia. Finally, since the only species of genus burchardia in NSW is Burchardia umbellata, we infer that this is Burchardia umbellata. This is also consistent with the results of the plant identification software.

Occurrence Remarks: Small tree to c. 1.9 m growing on slope close to river. Growing with Erigeron karvinskianus, Ehrharta erecta, Dodonaea triquetra, Pteridium esculentum, Pittosporum undulatum, Ceratopetalum gummiferum, Dianella, Casuarina gluaca, Oplismenus, Modiola caroliniana, Polyscias sambucifolia, Phyllanthus tenellus. In addition to this larger individual, I counted at least 50 small saplings (30-50 cm tall) naturalised along this stretch of the river for the next 600 m heading southwards, growing both amongst mangroves (riverward side) and in the dry sclerophyll forest on sandstone (landward side). Occurrence Remarks: Small erect herb to 20-25 cm tall, c. 15 plants naturalised, scattered along a 15 m stretch of gutter, growing in a thick layer of silt deposited along the gutter by recent flooding after heavy rain. Most plants with buds or finished flowers, with a single open flower, bright yellow. First photographed in morning at 10 am but collected at 3 pm same day, with open flower strongly wilted. Growing with Poa annua, Bidens pilosa, Sonchus oleraceus, Polycarpon tetraphyllum. There are several garden beds 15-20 m further along the street with plantings of this species, clearly the naturalisation source. Link to photographic voucher (iNaturalist): https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/217837052. Collected under licence SL100750.
Locality: Clapham Road, c. 50 m from intersection with Mary Street, Regents Park.

Occurrence Remarks: (Monocot) Flower bases of 6, very typical parallel leaf veins, suggesting a monocotyledon. The synephridium suggests that it may be a plant of the order Liliaceae. However, after repeated and careful screening with plant identification software and against images of confirmed observations available on plant net and iNat, we believe that this may in fact be Dianella caerulea, commonly known as Blue flax-lily, in the family Asphodelaceae. very characteristic reflexed petals, very characteristic buds with yellow structures on the margins, racemes, purple oval berries, and overall a very recognisable flower. It is worth noting that this family does not appear to be recorded in the Robinson Book under "Monocots", so I think this family, and this species, may be of very good and unique identification value, and I hope you will draw attention to it. Our Alfalfa plants are herbaceous, with berries, anthers that do not curl after dehiscence, and stamens whose filaments are inflated and papillate at the tips. The flowers are strongly tubular and of mixed reddish-brown-orange colour. Anthers dehiscent through apical pores, filaments attached at or near the base of the anthers, anthers inactive. Leaf blades spreading, flowers borne in axils or not alone at apices; plants non-alpine types. Leaves mostly basal or reduced and bracteate along above-ground stems, flowers often borne on nearly leafless scapes or apical inflorescences. Underground stems are well developed, usually bulbs, corms, tubers or rhizomes. This agrees with Genus Dianella as described by plantnet. Our Alfalfa family has inflorescences that clearly exceed the height of the leaf blades; leaf margins and midveins are scabrous at least at the base of the leaf; and grows in non-marine environments. Plants yellowish green or greyish green, with anthers longer than the expanded part of the filaments; fruit more than 4 mm long, shorter than or equal to its width; leaf margins smooth or minutely spiny. Leaf sheaths folded, usually with distinct keel-like ridges on the lower surface. Vein spacing on the lower surface of the leaf blade greater than or equal to the width of the veins, without papillae; anthers yellow, yellow-brown or blue. Leaf sheaths cover more than half. A comparison using plantnet's key locates Dianella caerulea, which is consistent with the results obtained by our previous plant identification software, so we deduce that this monocotyledon is Dianella caerulea. We found this plant in the right hand direction on Burns Rd at Picnic Point on our way into Georges River National Park. Given that Blue flax-lily occurs in a wide range of habitats and is easy to grow, I think it makes sense that it shows off in that area.

This plant is a monocotyledons, as shown in the parallel venation of the leaves. It is part of the Liliaceae family as it is a tufted herb. This particular species is Dianella caerulea. This plant grows in woodlands on sandstone. It has blue flowers with yellow antlers.

Occurrence Remarks: I have depicted this flower as a part of the Iridaceae family due to the fact that it contains 2 different types of petals which is a common aspect of the Iridaceae family. The three outer petals have a yellow strip in the middle which is only present on half of the petal. Whereas, the inner petal is mostly white with aspects of yellow towards the base. There is also 3 purple, petal like structures at the center of the flower which matches the description of the genus Dietes. The flower is radially symmetrical and also contains an inferior ovary. It forms a bush like structure, where the length of the stem is quite long and clean as it ends in 1 or more fortnight lily flowers. The leaves are a long thin strip like structure with a pointed end. It is connected from the base of the plant and contains parallel veins indicating it is a monocot plant type. The dead flowers form a hard shell like structure where there petal like structures which is hollow on the inside.

Scattered plants along shaded grassy bank, fruiting, to c. 1 m high. Growing with Syncarpia glomulifera, Melaleuca styphelioides, Asaparagus aethiopicus, Cayratia clematidea, Rubus parvifolius, Indigofera australis, Trema tomentosa, Oplismenus, Sarcopetalum harveyanum. Naturalised individuals and small patches scattered throughout the reserve, mostly in shaded and/or damp places. Link to photographic voucher (iNaturalist): https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/169736335. Collected under licence SL100750.

In the genus Dillwynia as the wing petals are very narrow in comparison to the banner petals. It also has simple and linear leaves with an alternate arrangement. In the species Dillwynia floribunda as it is a small erect shrub that has a hairy stem and has its inflorescence on a peduncle. I’ve excluded Dillwynia retorta as this plant appears to have more crowded leaves.

Occurrence Remarks: Growing off foot path on both sides of area, wrapped around a young sprouting beefwood, heart seeds dominate the area.

This species is Hardenbergia violacea, from the family Fabaceae and genus Hardenbergia. It is in the family Fabaceae as it’s leaves are arranged alternately and its flowers which are zygomorphic. The genus is Hardenbergia as it is a climbing plant, with alternate, compound leaves that have been modified to be 1-foliate. Its flowers consist of a standard petal, 2 wings and a keel. This is the species Hardenbergia violacea. Some stems are upright while others are climbing. Leaves are long, simple and dark green - and narrow-lanceolate shaped. They are arranged alternately along the stem, and have strongly reticulate venation. The flowers produced are purple, with a yellow/green centre on its 2 standard petals.
Purple Hardenbergias next to a white one (previous post)
White Hardenbergia in a cluster of purple Hardenbergias (next post)
Climber. >2 m long. Purple flowers. Entwined on low-lying shrubs.

Occurrence Remarks: This is labeled Hibbertia sp. undescribed.
Locality: Henry Lawson Drive, Waterboard Land, Picnic Point.

Occurrence Remarks: Semi-prostrate subshrub 8-14 cm high. Calyx pale green, with whitish hooked hairs on outer surface. Corolla yellow. Stamens 12, arranged to one side of ovary, staminodes absent; carpels 2, glabrous; styles 2. Fruits nor seen. [Tim Hammer, State Herbarium for South Australia, Leaf tissue sampled for DNA analysis, Nov 2022].
Habitat: Subpopulation A of Hibbertia glabrescens. Mowed area near western end of runways, with Lomandra longifolia, Kunzia ambigua and Acacia suaveolens.

Occurrence Remarks: Locally frequent prostrate shrub 10 cm x 1 m. Flowers yellow (few remaining). Fruits turning brown after dispersal. Seeds collected from c. 10 plants. VOUCHER for Millennium Seed Bank Project.
Habitat: Flat landform, kept slashed on glide path to main runway. Area dominated by Themeda australis and Eragrostis curvula, occasional Kunzea ambigua, Acacia suaveolens, A. genistifolia. Deep grey brown sandy alluvium.
Locality: North western sector of Bankstown Airport (area 5, below northwest flight path).
North western sector of Bankstown Airport (area 5, below northwest flight path).

Occurrence Remarks: Locally common woody, spreading, procumbent sub-shrub to 15cm. Commonly growing in tangled clumps, hard to identify individual plants. Flowers yellow. Cuttings taken from 3 subpopulations.
Habitat: In cleared grassland adjacent to remnant river flat forest, potentially former Scribbly Gum Woodland community. Found in open aspects in better drained soils in modifeid (slashed) grassland. Soils loamy sands over alluvial deposits/sandstone. With Kunzea ambigua, Eragrostis curvula, Hypericum gramineum, Pasture grasses, Plantago sp, regenerating Banksia integrifolia.
Locality: Paddock off NW end of Bankstown Airport runway (Area 5) in centre of paddock, access off Rabaul Rd, Bankstown
Recorded By: Phillips, G.P. | Errington, G. | Cuneo, P.V.

Occurrence Remarks: Locally frequent low prostrate shrub to 10cm high by 1m across. Flowers yellow, fruits green ripening to dark brown. Conservation seed collection made with OEH Saving Our Species project for future translocation. Approx 25 mature plants in this sub-population.
Habitat: Flat open grassland dominated by Eragrostis curvula and Themeda triandra with occasional regrowth shrubs of Kunzea ambigua, Banksia integrifolia. Area routinely slashed. Soils fine grey sandy alluvium with increasing clay at depth.
Locality: NW sector of Bankstown Airport, fenced conservation zone in area 5 below NW flight path, LHS of site, ~30m from creekline
Recorded By: Cuneo, P.V. | Willis, K.E. | Sherieff, A.

This species is the Hibbertia scandens, from the Dilleniaceae family and Hibbertia genus. Dilleniaceae consists of species with alternate, simple and entire leaves. Its flowers are actinomorphic and mostly yellow, with 5 sepals and 5 petals. The genus Hibbertia contains flowers with stamens that are numerous and free - its filaments are not united into a tube. The species Hibbertia scandens is a climbing species with long stems. Its leaves are obovate, simple, base tapering and are arranged alternately along the stem. Its leaf margins are entire. Its flowers are yellow, with numerous stamens surrounding few carpels.

Occurrence Remarks: This plant is in the Proteaceae family due to its alternatign pinnatisect leaves and inflorescences. In the genus Isopogon due to its spike-like inflorescence. I've identified it as Isopogon anemonifolius based on the leaf pattern and arrangement as well as the flowers matching the decription on Plantnet. Other plants have also been seen around the area. The other possible species is Isopogon anethifolius but I've excluded it because its leaves are too thin.

Very distinctive flowers and flower heads, the flower axis is shortened into a coiled inflorescence, and the leaves are alternate. There are four tepals, which is a very typical feature of Proteaceae. The plant has dense globose or cylindrical inflorescences, the flowers are sessile and closely arranged, and the bracts become woody when they bear fruit. The inflorescence axis is usually less than 5 cm, the fruits are radiate or bilaterally symmetrical nuts, and the leaves are usually divided into multiple segments or a few are entire. The fruit falls off with the bracts, the nut is not significantly flattened, the flower head is inflorescence, and the perianth tube is not completely split to the base. It is consistent with the description of the plantnet, and it can be judged that it belongs to the genus Isopogon. The leaves are usually divided into flat or cylindrical segments. In rare cases, the leaves below the inflorescence are intact, and the leaves are linear and less than 5 mm wide. The width of the divided segments of the leaves exceeds 1 mm and often exceeds 3 mm; the plant grows in an upright or spreading posture. The perianth is yellow and hairless except for a tuft of short hairs at the top. The leaves are usually no more than 9 cm long, the length of the undivided part is roughly equal to the divided part, the width of the divided part is 3-5 mm, usually only the midrib is obvious or all veins are not obvious, and the end is not sharp; the perianth length is about 10-12 mm, consistent with the description of the plantnet, it can be judged to be Isopogon anemonifolius. In addition, based on the comparison with the Proteaceae column in Robinson Book, we think our view is correct. The plant does have a very characteristic spherical woody cone, which is a typical feature of the genus isopogon. The height of its shrub is not high, just over one meter, so we can also rule out isopogon anetbifolius, which is taller (to 3m). So it can only be Isopogon anemonifolius.

Specimen showing the xerophytic character of reduction of leaf surface owing to unfavourable conditions. The plant from which the leaves were taken was growing on the plateau overlooking Cooks River at Undercliffe, in a shallow depression with a few inches of shale covering the rock which after rain becomes a pool of stagnant water.
Shrub 2-3 feet [0.6-0.9 m]. Reduced leaf division.

[All these qualities can be observed within the photographs.] Firstly, this plant has distinct qualities of the Myrtaceae family; woody shrub, simple entire leaves with oil glands, actinomorphic flowers with 5 petals, a half inferior ovary and numerous showy stamens. Secondly, it has distinct qualities of the Genus Kunzea; dehiscent fruit, flower buds without calyptras, free stamens that exceed petals in length, alternate leaves, thin leaves (<5mm wide), persistent sepals and flowers on leaf axils. Although Genus Kunzea and Leptospermum appear similar, the filaments of Kunzea exceed petal length unlike Leptospermum (filaments shorter than petals), hence why the plant is Genus Kunzea. Thirdly, it has distinct qualities of the species Kunzea ambigua; white flowers crowded near leaves, short pedicels and villous young stems. While Kunzea axillaris and Kunzea occidentalis are similar to K. ambigua, K. axillaris has far shorter leaves (3-5mm compared to 4-12mm) and K. occidentalis has more glabrous young stems. Extra Info: K. ambigua has a distinctly strong and enjoyable smell. Also, Les Robinson speculates that the term "ambigua" (meaning doubt in Latin) indicates the founders' original confusion with this species regarding its classification as Kunzea or Leptospermum. References include Field Guide to the Native Plants by Les Robinson (2003) and PlantNET. Photographed during the day.

Occurrence Remarks: Clade: Monocots Family: Asparagaceae Genus: Lomandra Species: Lomandra hystrix (green mat-rush) - This species is in the Asparagaceae family as it is a shrub. Another trait which identifies this species in the Asparagaceae family is that it has long, hairless leaves with parallel venation. - This species is in the genus Lomandra as it contains long and narrow leaves which resemble blades. Furthermore, the base of the plant does not contain a stem. - Another feature which places this species in the Asparagaceae family is the fact that its flowers are arranged in whorled inflorescences. - Each inflorescence contains a cluster of spiky bracts. The flowers are very small and either white or cream coloured. - Lomandra hystrix is very similar to Lomandra longifolia, though I have excluded this possibility through the fact that the leaves of this species is pointed at the end, whereas the leaves of Lomandra longifolia end in a ‘W’ shape. - Yet another feature which distinguishes this species from L.longifolia is the fact that its flowers are in branched inflorescences (which are also open and loose), whereas the flowers of L.longifolia are not branched (as observed on Plantnet)

(Re-submit) The corolla of the plant is obviously butterfly-shaped, with very distinct characteristics of the Fabaceae Fabaceae subfamily. It can be directly judged from the appearance of the flower that it belongs to the Fabaceae Fabaceae subfamily. The leaves of the plant are all single leaves, simple, degenerate or missing. The leaves are simple leaves, without stipules or separate stipules. The stamens are free structures. The two teeth on the upper part of the sepals are not fused into a wide notched lip, and the three teeth on the lower part are very small and narrow. The bracteoles are large, rounded, and easy to fall off; the leaves are tiny and also easy to fall off. The pods are spherical, and the inner part of the ovary is separated by a longitudinal septum, or the surface of the pods has longitudinal grooves. After comparing with plantnet, it can be confirmed that this is a plant of the genus Mirbelia. The leaves of the plant are 2 to 10 mm long, with a small recurved tip at the top. The leaves are linear, sometimes oblong or narrowly ovate, and are 1 to 5 mm wide. The upper surface of the leaves has a distinct reticular texture. After comparing it with plantnet, I can confirm that it is Mirbelia rubiifolia. In addition, using Robinson Book to search under the genus Mirbelia in the leguminous family, I can find that there are only two plants, and the other plant is a slender, erect shrub, and 1m high, which is completely different from the plant I obtained, so it can be ruled out. So it can also be confirmed that it is Mirbelia rubiifolia.

Occurrence Remarks: Very typical red *Oxalis*, including typical unlined perfect spiral basal trifoliate leaves, petioles with characteristic hairs, corolla fused from the bottom and 5 flower bases. Most importantly, after taking out a small amount of its leaves for tasting, it has a very typical sour taste of *Oxalis*, which suggests that it is a kind of *Oxalis*. Because its corolla is purple-red, based on experience, we judge that this is *Oxalis corymbosa*. Because the characteristics of the *Oxalidaceae* family are relatively complex, including not only *Oxalis corymbosa*, but also woody plants such as carambola, and the identification characteristics of this plant are too obvious, so we skipped the stage of using the key and directly identified this plant as *Oxalis corymbosa*. We found this *Oxalis corymbosa* by a road in the north of Panania. When we found it, it had only two flowers, and the distribution range was not large, and the settlement was isolated. Note: The clover of the Oxalis family and the clover of the Leguminosae family look different and have their own characteristics, so they can be distinguished. Although Oxalis latifolia is also similar to the plant we obtained, its compound leaves are shaped like arrows(or triangles), which is not align with the plant we found. Thus we can conclude that it is Oxalis corymbosa.
First time this sp. of Oxalis has popped up in this part of the yard, but present elsewhere on the property.

Occurrence Remarks: [All these qualities can be observed within the photographs.] Firstly, this plant has distinct qualities of the Euphorbiaceae family; woody shrub with alternate leaves and fruit within a schizocarpic 3 chambered ball. Unfortunately, there were no flowers at the time. Secondly, it has distinct qualities of the Genus Ricinus; encapsulated fruit with caruncles, wide peltate leaves with toothed margins and is 7-9 palmately lobed. Thirdly, it is the species Ricinus communis as it is the only species of the genus Ricinus in the world. Otherwise, the red caruncles, green fruit and absent stipules are also features of R. communis. Extra info: The product castor oil is derived from the seeds of this plant. However, these seeds also contain a toxin called ricin, therefore raw seeds should ideally not be consumed. References include Field Guide to the Native Plants by Les Robinson (2003) and PlantNET. Photographed during the day.

Occurrence Remarks: [All these qualities can be observed within the photographs.] Firstly, this plant has distinct qualities of the Fabaceae family; woody shrub, legumes as fruit and flowers with 5 free petals. This plant is of the Fabaceae subfamily, Caesalpinioideae as the flowers are irregular with a non-papilionaceous corolla and equally sized petals. Secondly, it has distinct qualities of the Genus Senna; absent spines/prickles, pinnately compound leaves, yellow petals and flat dehiscent pods. Thirdly, it has distinct qualities of the species Senna didymobotrya; 7-15 leaflet pairs per leaf, absent glands on leaves, tall raceme inflorescence with dark brown bracts, 2 conspicuous anthers and oblong pods with depressions between the seeds. All other Senna species do not have as tall of a raceme and have much lighter coloured bracts. Extra info: This plant is commonly referred to as the popcorn plant as rubbing the leaves will bring about the scent of buttered popcorn, however, it does depend on the person. References include Field Guide to the Native Plants by Les Robinson (2003) and PlantNET. Photographed during the day.

Occurrence Remarks: [All these qualities can be observed within the photographs.] Firstly, this plant has distinct qualities of the family Solanaceae; woody shrub, purple flowers with 5 petals and berries as fruit. Secondly, it has distinct qualities of the genus Solanum; pinnatisect leaves, firm berries and stellate, purple, 5 lobed flowers in a cymose/panicle-like inflorescence (Fig 5). Thirdly, it has distinct qualities of the species Solanum aviculare; non-climbing, erect, light violet corolla, entire margins with leaf length at 2-8 times as its width, leaves are either lobed or entire with a stalk, egg-shaped berries and mostly glabrous on all surfaces. This species is commonly confused with Solanum laciniatum. However, the above pictures show no notches in the corolla lobes. It is also confused with Solanum vescum which unlike S. aviculare has a spherical shaped berry and stalkless leaves. Unfortunately, the berries aren’t ripe, and the final colour isn’t known to be able to effectively use the key. Hence the focus is on the berries shape and leaves. Extra info: The common name, Kangaroo apple is inspired by the shape of the leaves which is thought to resemble a kangaroo’s foot. Whilst the scientific name ‘aviculare’ refers to little bird in Latin after the wing-like appendages on the leaves. References include Field Guide to the Native Plants by Les Robinson (2003) and PlantNET. Photographed during the day.

Using the description provided by PlantNET the plant would be: In the family Solanaceae due to it having simple pinnate leaves that are alternate, a calyx that is campanulate and a five lobed corolla that is stellate. In the genus Solanum because there appears to be 5 stamens that each have anthers that are 2-locular and basifixed. In image 4 the 5 stamens may be difficult to confirm, however the angle of the image and the symmetry of the plant could allow me to infer that the remaining 2 stamens were out of shot. For the presence of there being 2 locular and basifixed anthers, the apparent bulge and openings of the anthers in image 5 is shown through the white outline that shows that there are two parts. This also shows that the bulge that divides the two appears to align between the stamen beneath them, which can help confirm that there are 5 stamens in total through the number of 2-locular anthers. In the species Solanum aviculare because it’s an erect shrub, has a violet corolla, entire leaves, and lacks prickles. I’ve rejected Solanum linearifolium as an option as it is not glabrous. I’ve also rejected Solanum vescum because the size of the leaf is different with our plant not having a measurement of 5 to 15 cm long and 0.5 to 1.3 cm wide.

Occurrence Remarks: [All these qualities can be observed within the photographs.] Firstly, this plant has distinct qualities of the family Commelinaceae; herbaceous monocot with conspicuous flowers in parts of 3 (6 tepals in 2 whorls of 3), a superior ovary and parallel veins in leaves. Secondly, it has distinct qualities of the genus Tradescantia; multiple pedicellate flower clusters enclosed with 2 large leafy bracts. Thirdly, it has distinct qualities of the species Tradescantia fluminensis; the dark green top surface of the leaves, the lighter green underside of the leaves, 3 free white inner tepals, 3 green outer tepals, 6 yellow anthers on filaments tufted with white hairs and no occurrence of fruit. It is unlikely to be the species Tradescantia zebrina which has pink tepals and purple on the underside of its leaves. Extra info: While amazing for groundcover, this plant is not ideal for native species conservation. The competitiveness of this plant has been incredibly damaging to our native habitats and plants. References include Field Guide to the Native Plants by Les Robinson (2003) and PlantNET. Photographed during the day.

Link to photographic voucher (iNaturalist): https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/172298254. Collected under licence SL100750.
Locality: Beauty Point Reserve, Georges River National Park.

Occurrence Remarks: Mature plants: all plants 20 - 40 cm with flowers and/or capsules. Flowering and fruiting: Flowers deep blues opening in sunshine. Capsules with distinct red lines. Mixture of larger clumps with several stems (underground rhizomes present) and smaller, single-stemmed plants. Flowers being visited by small moths/butterflies, Flowers and fruit looked consistent between plants, no evidence of hybridisation. Measurements from fresh flowers: Calyx 3.5 mm with lobes 1 mm long; corolla tube 1 - 1.5 mm long; lobes ovate, deep blues, 3.5 mm long; capsules narrow, c. 10 mm long with deep red lines; seeds very small, smooth, brown, glossy.
Habitat: Low-lying area several metres from patches of Melaleuca decora. Plants found in open, grassy area adjacent to dry pond. Clay soil. The area is often under water after rain. Strong mesic component in understorey. Grassy understorey 40 - 60 cm high. Dense growth of couch with range of taller grasses and herbs. Associates: Native species: Cynodon dactylon, Dichelachne micrantha, Agrostis avenacea, Centella asiatica, Juncus usitatus, Senecio quadridentatus, S. hispidulus, Cheilanthes sieberi, Cyperus sp., Epilobium billardierianum. Exotic species: Briza subaristata, Briza major, Pennisetum clandestinum, Senecio madagascariensis, Verbena bonariensis, Conyza sp.
Locality: NE corner of area 3b of the Chullora lands, between the main rail line N of area 3 and smaller rail siding extending into area 3.

Occurrence Remarks: Population over 7 m x 3 m. 7 plants seen. 3 large plants, other smaller along track among taller grasses. All plants flowering. Young fruits. 10-40 cm high, scattered. Flowers blue. See specimen sheet for photo of site and threats.
Habitat: Growing along grassy track and edge. Track regularly maintained by mowing/slashing or use. Site open and disturbed, c. 30 m from creek line. Growing with: Briza subaristata, Senecio madagascariensis, Eragrostis curvula, Pennisetum clandestinum, Plantaago lanceolata, Lachnagrostis filiformis, Dillwynia sieberi, Acacia longifolia, Cassinia arcuata.

Occurrence Remarks: Site no. 3-1. First located 28 Oct 2002, revisited 12 Nov 2002, 17 Mar 2003. On 28 Oct 2002: Mature plants, all plants 20-40 cm high with flowers and/or capsules. Flowers deep blue opening in sunshine. Capsules have distinct red lines. On 17 Mar 2003 early season growth now dead but some new regrowth from older stems evident on most plants. Flowers, buds and fruit. Mixture of larger clumps with several stems (underground rhizomes present) and smaller, single stemmed plants. Several plants of W. gracilis recorded in Mar on upper slope in more open area with exposed soil. See more notes and photo of site with specimen sheet.
Habitat: Low-lying area between main rail line and siding, several metres N of small stand of Melaleuca decora. Plants found in open, grassy area adjacent to dry pond. After heavy rains this area often saturated or with standing water. Clay soils. Dominated by couch with a range of taller grasses and herbs. A mixture of native and exotic plant species. Associated species: Cynodon dactylon, Dichelachne mictantha, Lachnagrostis filiformis, Centella asiatica, Juncus usitatus, Senecio quadridentatis, S. hispidulus, Cheilanthes sieberi, Epilobium billardierianum subsp. cinereum, Wahlenbergia gracilis, Goodenia paniculata, Eragrostis brownii, Alternanthera denticulata, Fimbristylis dichotoma, Briza subaristata, B. major, Pennisetum clandestinum, Senecio madagascariensis, Cyperus eragrostis, Verbena bonariensis, Conyza albida, Bidens pilosa, Cirsium vulgare, Aster subulatus, Echinochloa crus-gallii. Extent of population 2 m x 2 m.
Locality: NE corner of area 3b of the Chullora lands, between the main rail line N of area 3 and smaller rail siding extending into area 3.

Occurrence Remarks: Site no. 3-2. First located 28 Oct 2002, revisited 12 Nov 2002, 17 Mar 2003. Two plants observed, one in Oct, a second in March. Mature plants. Plants c. 30 cm high. Original plant observed in Oct appeared dead in Mar, however, green shoots seen at base. Second plant observed in Mar appeared quite green. Fruiting in Oct only, mature capsules. Second plant observed in Mar with buds and young capules. This site is c. 100 m SW of site 3-1. Several small plants of W. gracilis were also observed during Mar survey, in flower and fruit. Seed likely to have been dispersed to this location in soil transported from another part of Area 3 or 2. Photo of site included.
Habitat: A narrow disturbed area. Mound of dirt covered with couch and range of weedy exotic species. Associated species: Cynodon dactylon, Cassinia arcuata, Centella asiatica, Wahlenbergia gracilis, Eragrostis curvula, Paspalum dilatatum, Setaria gracilis, Sida rhombifolia, Senecio madagascariensis, Plantago lanceolatus, Conyza albida. Extent of population 2 m x 2 m.
Locality: NE corner of area 3b of the Chullora lands, between the main rail line N of area 3 and access road.
